rows.title: King of Piel
rows.evidence: The Piel Island article says the council selects the King of Piel, the landlord of the island's public house.
rows.summary: Piel Island lies in Morecambe Bay, around 1⁄2 mile (800 metres) off the southern tip of the Furness peninsula in the administrative county of Cumbria, England. The council's administrative duties also include the selection of the "King" of Piel, who is the landlord of the island's public house, the Ship Inn. The landlord of the Ship Inn pub is known as 'The King of Piel', a title instituted in the 19th century and harking back to Lambert Simnel and his attempt to usurp the English throne.

rows.title: Knighthood of Piel
rows.evidence: The Piel Island article calls the Knighthood of Piel a tradition handed down by fishermen, carried out at the inn on the island.
rows.summary: Piel Island lies in Morecambe Bay, around 1⁄2 mile (800 metres) off the southern tip of the Furness peninsula in the administrative county of Cumbria, England. The council's administrative duties also include the selection of the "King" of Piel, who is the landlord of the island's public house, the Ship Inn. A tradition handed down by fishermen for centuries is the 'Knighthood of Piel'. In a room of the inn is a large oak chair and anyone who sits in it is made a 'Knight of Piel'. The ceremonial knighting is carried out by the King of Piel or a fellow knight.

rows.title: Unst Bus Shelter
rows.evidence: The Unst Bus Shelter article places the shelter at Baltasound on Unst and says local volunteers furnish it and redecorate it periodically.
rows.reject_reason: The article describes a furnished bus shelter that volunteers redecorate. That is not a custom, festival, dance, or craft. The photograph shows an identifiable person sitting in the shelter.
rows.summary: The Unst Bus Shelter, also known as Bobby's Bus Shelter, is a bus shelter and bus stop near the village of Baltasound, on the isle of Unst, Shetland Islands, Scotland. The local council had plans to remove the bus shelter in 1996, but after the seven-year-old sent them a letter asking them not to and explaining that the shelter is where he kept his bike while at school, the council left it there and local volunteers furnished and decorated it. It is furnished and redecorated periodically. For example, in 2010 it was given World Cup themed decoration due to Macaulay's visit to South Africa to see the 2010 FIFA World Cup, and each year by local residents with a sofa, television, computer and other home comforts.

rows.title: Sabbath observance
rows.evidence: The Isle of Lewis article says Lewis is the northern part of Lewis and Harris and that Sabbath observance is kept, with most shops and licensed premises closed.
rows.summary: The Isle of Lewis or simply Lewis is the northern part of Lewis and Harris, the largest island of the Western Isles or Outer Hebrides archipelago in Scotland. Today, life is very different from elsewhere in Scotland, with Sabbath observance, the Scottish Gaelic language and peat cutting retaining more importance than elsewhere. The Sabbath is generally observed, with most shops and licensed premises closed on that day, although there has been a scheduled air service to mainland Scotland as well as a scheduled ferry service since 19 July 2009.

rows.title: Peat cutting
rows.evidence: The Isle of Lewis article says peat was traditionally cut on the island and that peat stacking follows local customs. It identifies Lewis as the northern part of Lewis and Harris.
rows.summary: The Isle of Lewis or simply Lewis is the northern part of Lewis and Harris, the largest island of the Western Isles or Outer Hebrides archipelago in Scotland. Today, life is very different from elsewhere in Scotland, with Sabbath observance, the Scottish Gaelic language and peat cutting retaining more importance than elsewhere. The interior of the island is a large area of moorland from which peat was traditionally cut as fuel, although this practice has become less common. Peat stacking also follows local customs and a well-built peat stack can be a work of art.

rows.title: Highland Games
rows.evidence: The Isle of Lewis article says Tong, near Stornoway, hosts the Highland Games each summer. It identifies Lewis, including Stornoway, as the northern part of Lewis and Harris.
rows.summary: The Isle of Lewis or simply Lewis is the northern part of Lewis and Harris, the largest island of the Western Isles or Outer Hebrides archipelago in Scotland. Due to its larger area and flatter, more fertile land, Lewis contains three-quarters of the population of the Western Isles, and the largest settlement, Stornoway. The village of Tong about 2 miles (3 km) from Stornoway plays host to the Highland Games and the Western Isles Strongest man competition each summer.

rows.title: Shinty
rows.evidence: The Isle of Lewis article says shinty was traditionally played on the island, died out, and was revived by Lewis Camanachd. It identifies Lewis as the northern part of Lewis and Harris.
rows.reject_reason: The Isle of Lewis article says shinty died out and was revived as a club that competes nationally, as it is played across Gaelic Scotland. A team sport is not a custom, festival, dance, or craft.
rows.summary: The Isle of Lewis or simply Lewis is the northern part of Lewis and Harris, the largest island of the Western Isles or Outer Hebrides archipelago in Scotland. Shinty which was traditionally played in the island as in the rest of the Scottish Gaelic-speaking areas of Scotland, died out by the mid-20th century at the latest. However, it was revived in the 1990s and there is now a strong local club known as Lewis Camanachd which competes in national competition.

rows.title: Harping
rows.evidence: The Gigha article describes a tradition of harping on Gigha, kept by the Galbraith family into the seventeenth century.
rows.reject_reason: The Gigha article says the island had a harping tradition whose family was thought to have remained until at least 1685. It does not describe a living practice.
rows.summary: Gigha ( GHEE-ə; Scottish Gaelic: Giogha; Scots: Gigha) or the Isle of Gigha (and formerly Gigha Island) is an island off the west coast of Kintyre in Scotland. Gigha had a vigorous tradition of harping, represented mainly by the family called Mac an Bhreatnaigh (Galbraith), who were active in Gigha and Kintyre, and it is thought that their descendants were in Gigha until at least 1685.
